case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Medicaid beneficiaries have a privately enforceable right of action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 to challenge a State's exclusion of a Medicaid provider under the free-choice-of-provider provision, 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23) — the Medicaid 'free-choice-of-provider' provision — read in conjunction with 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which provides a cause of action for deprivation of federal statutory rights under color of state law.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: South Carolina (Petitioner) argues that § 1396a(a)(23) does not unambiguously confer an individually enforceable right upon Medicaid beneficiaries sufficient to sustain a § 1983 cause of action, that the Secretary of HHS — not private litigants — is the proper enforcement mechanism through funding withholding under 42 U.S.C. § 1396c, and that the Fourth Circuit's prior rulings should be reconsidered in light of the Supreme Court's decision in Talevski and evolving precedent on implied private rights of action. Supporting amici, including 311 state legislators, 108 South Carolina legislators, the Life Legal Defense Foundation, and the United States as amicus curiae, further contend that allowing private enforcement undermines state sovereignty over Medicaid administration and creates confusion in the enforcement framework.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Planned Parenthood South Atlantic (Respondent) argues that § 1396a(a)(23) unambiguously creates an individual right for Medicaid beneficiaries to choose among qualified providers, that this right is privately enforceable through § 1983 consistent with binding precedents such as Wilder v. Virginia Hospital Ass'n and Blessing v. Freestone, and that the Supreme Court's decision in Talevski reaffirmed rather than undermined the framework for § 1983 enforcement of Medicaid provisions, thereby leaving the Fourth Circuit's prior determinations intact.
key_precedents: Health & Hospital Corp. of Marion County v. Talevski, 599 U.S. 166 (2023)
Wilder v. Virginia Hospital Ass'n, 496 U.S. 498 (1990)
Kerr v. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic, 143 S. Ct. 2633 (2023) (GVR order)
42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(28) and § 1396r (FNHRA provisions at issue in Talevski)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett's structural argument continues to give me genuine pause, and I want to be transparent that I find it the most intellectually serious challenge to my position — but after three rounds of deliberation, I remain unpersuaded that structural framing alone can override operative text that Gonzaga's own framework would recognize as rights-conferring. The phrase 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any qualified provider of his choice' is grammatically centered on the individual beneficiary's freedom of action, and as Justice Jackson correctly emphasizes, Gonzaga directs us to the provision's operative language rather than its structural home in the statute. My minimalist instinct is to hold narrowly — this specific 'of his choice' language clears Gonzaga's bar, full stop — without resolving the deeper questions Justice Thomas raises about § 1983's application to Spending Clause statutes generally or what Justice Barrett's concurrence in Talevski left open. As the opinion-assigning Justice in a 6-3 configuration, I would assign the majority to Justice Kagan with instructions to write as narrowly as possible, confining the holding to this provision's specific text and expressly declining to address whether all Medicaid provisions or all Spending Clause statutes with beneficiary-focused language similarly confer § 1983 rights.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan argues that § 1396c's funding-withholding mechanism is insufficiently comprehensive to foreclose § 1983 enforcement because it operates at the programmatic level rather than providing individual remedies — but this argument inverts the proper analytical sequence under Gonzaga. The threshold question is not whether § 1396c forecloses § 1983, but whether § 1396a(a)(23) unambiguously confers an individually enforceable right in the first instance; the provision is structured as a condition on state Medicaid plans ('a State plan for medical assistance must provide'), not as a direct grant of rights to beneficiaries, and the 'any qualified provider of his choice' language describes the scope of the programmatic condition rather than unambiguously creating a personal entitlement. Justice Gorsuch's textualist reading of 'his choice' as unmistakably individual-centric is the most serious challenge to my position, but even rights-adjacent language embedded in a Spending Clause condition directed at state plan requirements does not satisfy Gonzaga's demanding bar — the provision speaks to what state plans must include, not to what individuals are guaranteed, and the contractual structure of Spending Clause legislation means that the 'rights' created run between the federal government and the states, not directly to beneficiaries. The existence of § 1396c as the designated enforcement mechanism, combined with the Spending Clause's contractual character that Justice Barrett correctly emphasized in her Talevski concurrence, confirms that Congress did not intend to supplement federal-state enforcement with private § 1983 suits that would disrupt state sovereignty over Medicaid program administration.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's textualist argument that 'any qualified provider of his choice' is grammatically structured around the beneficiary's entitlement is the most formidable challenge to my position, and I acknowledge it has genuine force — but it conflates rights-adjacent language with the unambiguous conferral of individually enforceable rights that Gonzaga demands. The critical structural point, which Justice Barrett correctly emphasizes, is that § 1396a frames the entire provision as what a 'State plan must provide' — Congress was legislating the federal-state relationship, and the 'his choice' language describes the scope of that programmatic condition rather than creating a self-executing personal entitlement enforceable through § 1983. Justice Kagan argues that § 1396c's funding-withholding mechanism is insufficiently comprehensive to foreclose § 1983, but this inverts the proper Gonzaga sequence — the threshold question is whether Congress unambiguously conferred an individually enforceable right at all, and the existence of § 1396c as the sole express remedy is strong evidence that Congress deliberately channeled enforcement through administrative mechanisms rather than private litigation. The six-justice majority's position would effectively transform every Spending Clause provision containing beneficiary-focused language into a § 1983 cause of action, precisely the result Gonzaga was designed to prevent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett's structural argument — that § 1396a's framing as what a 'State plan must provide' signals federal-state rather than individual rights — remains the most serious challenge, but after three rounds of deliberation I am more convinced than ever that it proves too much: as Justice Kagan correctly observes, accepting that framing wholesale would effectively nullify Gonzaga's own 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited' inquiry, since virtually every Medicaid provision is structured as a state plan requirement. The operative language 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any qualified provider of his choice' is grammatically and semantically centered on the individual beneficiary — the possessive 'his choice' is not bureaucratic boilerplate describing state administrative obligations but personal, possessive language that Gonzaga itself would recognize as unmistakably focused on the benefited class. Justice Thomas's deeper structural argument that Spending Clause 'rights' run only between the federal government and states is intellectually serious, but as I emphasized in joining Talevski's majority, that structural feature is not categorically dispositive where Congress has written in terms of personal entitlement, and I will not accomplish through this case what the Court expressly declined to do in Talevski. Finally, Justice Jackson correctly identifies that § 1396c's blunt funding-withholding mechanism provides zero individual remedy to a Medicaid beneficiary denied provider access today, and under Sea Clammers, foreclosure of § 1983 requires a remedial scheme that actually serves the individual plaintiff — a standard this intergovernmental fiscal tool cannot meet.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett's structural argument remains the most serious challenge, but after three rounds of deliberation I am more confident, not less, that it cannot bear the weight she places on it. Gonzaga's operative test asks whether the provision is 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited' — and as Justice Jackson correctly emphasizes, that inquiry focuses on the operative language, not the provision's structural home within a state-plan-requirements section. The phrase 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any qualified provider of his choice' is grammatically centered on the individual's freedom of action in a way that 'his choice' makes unmistakably personal, and Justice Barrett's own Talevski concurrence preserved Wilder rather than overruling it, which forecloses the argument that free-choice-of-provider language categorically fails Gonzaga. Justice Thomas's deeper argument that Spending Clause rights run only between the federal government and states is intellectually serious, but Talevski's majority — which I authored — expressly declined to make that structural feature categorically dispositive, and I will not accomplish through this case what the Court refused to do frontally there; the 6-3 tally here reflects that the individual-centric text of § 1396a(a)(23) clears Gonzaga's bar, and § 1396c's blunt programmatic remedy provides no basis under Sea Clammers for inferring that Congress foreclosed the private enforcement necessary to give this right practical meaning.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett's structural argument — that § 1396a frames the entire provision as what a 'State plan must provide,' suggesting Congress was legislating the federal-state relationship rather than creating personal entitlements — remains the most formidable challenge to my position, and I acknowledge it has genuine textualist force. However, after careful engagement with her argument, I return to the operative grammatical structure: the provision says an 'individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance... of his choice,' and Gonzaga's own test asks whether the provision is 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited' with 'unmistakable focus on the benefited class' — this language clears that bar. Justice Thomas's deeper originalist challenge about whether § 1983 was ever designed to enforce Spending Clause rights is the argument I find most intellectually serious and have flagged in prior writings, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, Talevski's majority declined to resolve that foundational question, and I am not prepared to use this case to make that structural leap when it would require overruling or substantially limiting decades of precedent without a majority for that proposition. I write separately to emphasize that the Court must eventually confront the Gonzaga/Talevski tension directly and provide clearer guidance on what 'unambiguous conferral' requires in the Spending Clause context, rather than leaving lower courts to navigate this doctrinal thicket case by case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett's structural argument — that § 1396a frames the entire provision as what a 'State plan must provide,' suggesting Congress was legislating the federal-state relationship rather than creating personal entitlements — remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I have wrestled with it carefully. However, Gonzaga's own framework instructs courts to look for provisions 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited,' and the phrase 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any qualified provider of his choice' is grammatically and semantically structured around the individual beneficiary's freedom of action, not around state administrative compliance obligations — a distinction Justice Gorsuch's textualist analysis correctly identifies. Justice Barrett is right that the Spending Clause's contractual character counsels caution, but as I noted in my prior reasoning, her own Talevski concurrence preserved rather than overruled Wilder, and the majority in Talevski declined to make the contractual structure of Spending Clause statutes categorically dispositive where individual-centric text is present. The asymmetry Justice Kagan identifies between § 1396c's blunt programmatic remedy and the individual harm suffered by a beneficiary denied provider access today remains a powerful structural signal that Congress contemplated private enforcement as a supplement — not a displacement — of administrative enforcement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Jackson press the strongest textual challenge — that 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any qualified provider of his choice' is grammatically centered on the individual beneficiary's freedom of action, and that Gonzaga's own test asks whether the provision is 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited.' I take this seriously and acknowledge the possessive 'his choice' has genuine individual-centric force. However, my Talevski concurrence's reasoning remains controlling for me: the Spending Clause's contractual character means that even beneficiary-focused language embedded in a state plan requirement describes what the federal-state bargain guarantees rather than directly vesting a self-executing personal entitlement in the beneficiary enforceable through § 1983, and Gonzaga demands unambiguous congressional intent to confer the latter. Justice Jackson's Sea Clammers point — that § 1396c's blunt programmatic remedy provides no individual relief and therefore cannot foreclose § 1983 — is textually plausible, but it conflates the foreclosure question with the threshold Gonzaga question: even if § 1396c does not foreclose private enforcement, that does not supply the affirmative unambiguous conferral of individually enforceable rights that Gonzaga independently requires, and the absence of an individual remedy in § 1396c is equally consistent with Congress having deliberately channeled enforcement through administrative mechanisms in a cooperative federalism structure.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett's structural argument remains the most serious challenge I face, but after three rounds of deliberation I am more confident, not less, that it cannot overcome the provision's operative text. Gonzaga's test is explicitly linguistic — it asks whether the provision is 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited' with 'unmistakable focus on the benefited class' — and the phrase 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any qualified provider of his choice' satisfies that test on its face regardless of the section's structural home in a state-plan-requirements provision. Justice Barrett's argument that 'his choice' merely describes the scope of a programmatic condition rather than vesting a personal entitlement would, as Justice Sotomayor correctly observes, effectively nullify Gonzaga's individual-centric language inquiry for virtually every Medicaid provision, since the entire statute is structured as state plan requirements — that cannot be the right reading of Gonzaga's framework. Finally, my background as a public defender reinforces what Justice Kagan's structural point makes clear: § 1396c's funding-withholding mechanism provides zero remedy to the individual denied provider access today, and Sea Clammers requires a remedial scheme that actually serves the individual plaintiff before § 1983 is foreclosed — a blunt intergovernmental fiscal tool does not meet that standard.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23) is phrased with unmistakable individual-centric focus — it grants beneficiaries the right 'to obtain' services 'from any institution, agency, or person qualified to perform the service' — satisfying Gonzaga's requirement of rights-creating language with an 'unmistakable focus on the benefited class.' Talevski reaffirmed rather than dismantled the § 1983 enforcement framework for Medicaid provisions, and Justice Barrett's concurrence notably preserved Wilder as valid precedent rather than interring it. While I am sympathetic to South Carolina's federalism concerns and the argument that § 1396c's administrative enforcement mechanism may be the preferred remedy, the narrow and institutionally responsible path here is to apply the Gonzaga/Talevski framework as written rather than use this case to broadly foreclose § 1983 enforcement of Spending Clause statutes — a step that would require overruling or substantially narrowing precedents this Court has repeatedly declined to explicitly overturn. The principle of judicial minimalism counsels against resolving more than the specific textual question presented, and on that question, § 1396a(a)(23)'s individual-rights-creating language is sufficiently clear to sustain the beneficiary's § 1983 claim.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist, I must first question whether § 1983, as originally enacted in 1871, was ever understood to encompass enforcement of federal statutory rights created through conditional spending grants to states — a question I have raised in prior writings and which the majority in Talevski declined to fully resolve. Setting aside that foundational concern, even under the Court's current framework, § 1396a(a)(23) does not unambiguously confer an individually enforceable right sufficient to sustain a § 1983 cause of action; the provision is framed as a condition on state Medicaid plans rather than a rights-conferring mandate directed at individual beneficiaries, and Congress expressly provided an enforcement mechanism through the Secretary's funding withholding authority under § 1396c, which strongly suggests Congress did not intend private enforcement. The Gonzaga framework demands that statutory text 'unambiguously' confer individual rights, and Spending Clause statutes face a 'significant hurdle' under Talevski precisely because the contractual nature of such legislation — between the federal government and the states — counsels against inferring private rights of action that disrupt state sovereignty and the cooperative federalism structure Congress deliberately constructed. Permitting Medicaid beneficiaries to privately enforce provider-qualification determinations through § 1983 effectively converts every Medicaid plan condition into a judicially enforceable individual entitlement, an outcome inconsistent with the original understanding of both § 1983 and the Spending Clause.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying the Gonzaga University v. Doe framework, which requires that a federal statute unambiguously confer an individually enforceable right with rights-creating language focused on the benefited class rather than the regulated entity, § 1396a(a)(23) is best read as a condition imposed on States participating in Medicaid rather than a clear conferral of individual rights on beneficiaries. The existence of an express enforcement mechanism in § 1396c — authorizing the Secretary to withhold federal funding from non-compliant States — strongly suggests Congress did not intend to create a parallel private enforcement regime through § 1983, consistent with the principle that comprehensive remedial schemes can foreclose implied private rights. While Talevski preserved § 1983 enforcement for certain Medicaid provisions, the majority's silence on Wilder and its reliance on Gonzaga's demanding 'unambiguous conferral' standard counsels skepticism toward extending private enforcement here, particularly given the significant federalism concerns raised by allowing private litigants to second-guess State determinations about provider qualifications — a matter traditionally within State administrative discretion over Medicaid program integrity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1396a(a)(23) unambiguously confers an individually enforceable right upon Medicaid beneficiaries by mandating that states provide freedom to obtain care from 'any qualified' provider — language that is unmistakably individual-centric and focused on the benefited class of Medicaid recipients, satisfying the Gonzaga/Talevski framework. Talevski reaffirmed that Spending Clause statutes can create privately enforceable rights under § 1983 and did not overrule Wilder, which specifically addressed Medicaid beneficiary rights; Justice Barrett's concurrence in Talevski acknowledged Wilder's continued validity without repudiating it. Relegating enforcement exclusively to the Secretary's funding-withholding mechanism under § 1396c would leave vulnerable low-income patients — the very population Medicaid was designed to protect — without a meaningful, timely remedy when states unlawfully exclude qualified providers, a result inconsistent with the remedial purposes of both Medicaid and § 1983. The practical reality that Medicaid beneficiaries often cannot wait for federal administrative enforcement proceedings, particularly when seeking time-sensitive reproductive healthcare, weighs heavily in favor of recognizing the private right of action that Congress plainly intended when it used rights-creating language directed at individual beneficiaries.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23) unambiguously confers an individual right on Medicaid beneficiaries to receive care 'from any institution, agency, community pharmacy, or person, qualified to perform the service or services required,' which satisfies the Blessing v. Freestone framework as reaffirmed — not overruled — by Talevski's majority opinion. In Talevski, the Court expressly declined to abandon § 1983 as an enforcement vehicle for Spending Clause statutes and applied the Blessing three-part test to uphold FNHRA rights, signaling that the framework remains operative where statutory text clearly focuses on the benefited individual. The § 1396c funding-withholding mechanism does not constitute the kind of 'comprehensive remedial scheme' that forecloses § 1983 enforcement under Middlesex County Sewerage Authority v. National Sea Clammers, as it operates at the programmatic level between the federal government and states rather than providing any individual remedy for a beneficiary wrongfully denied provider choice. While I am attentive to South Carolina's workability and state sovereignty concerns, the pragmatic solution is to hold that the clear individual-rights language of § 1396a(a)(23) sustains § 1983 enforcement, leaving Congress — not this Court — to restructure the remedial framework if it chooses.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Applying the Gonzaga/Talevski framework with genuine textualist rigor, 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23)'s 'any qualified provider of his choice' language is unmistakably individual-centric and rights-creating — it speaks directly to the beneficiary ('his choice'), not merely to aggregate programmatic goals, satisfying the requirement that the provision be 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited' with an 'unmistakable focus on the benefited class.' Talevski, 599 U.S. at 183. The plain meaning of 'any qualified provider of his choice' confers a discrete, individually held entitlement rather than a mere programmatic condition, distinguishing it from the diffuse benefit provisions that failed the Gonzaga test in cases like Blessing v. Freestone. While South Carolina correctly notes that § 1396c provides a federal enforcement mechanism, Talevski reaffirmed that the existence of such a mechanism does not automatically foreclose § 1983 enforcement where Congress has unambiguously conferred an individual right, and the text here clears that bar. I write separately to note that Armstrong's repudiation of Wilder's 'relatively loose standard' is well-taken, but applying the stricter Gonzaga standard to this specific provision's individualized language still yields enforcement for the beneficiary.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1396a(a)(23) contains unmistakably individual-centric, rights-creating language — it provides that any Medicaid beneficiary 'may obtain' services from 'any institution, agency, community pharmacy, or person, qualified to perform the service,' which is precisely the kind of provision 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited' that Gonzaga University v. Doe and Talevski identify as sufficient to sustain a § 1983 cause of action. While Armstrong repudiated the broader implication of § 1983 actions that Wilder exemplified, and the circuit split reflects genuine doctrinal uncertainty, the free-choice-of-provider provision is meaningfully distinguishable from the reimbursement-rate provision at issue in Wilder because it speaks directly to individual beneficiaries' entitlements rather than to systemic program administration. The Secretary's enforcement mechanism under § 1396c does not, under our precedents, automatically foreclose § 1983 enforcement absent a sufficiently comprehensive remedial scheme that demonstrates congressional intent to preclude private suits, and funding withholding is a blunt instrument that provides no meaningful remedy to an individual beneficiary who is denied access to a chosen provider today. As an institutionalist, I am also mindful that the Court's GVR in Kerr v. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic signals that Talevski's framework warrants fresh application here, and that disrupting settled reliance interests of millions of Medicaid beneficiaries who have long understood this provision as conferring an enforceable individual right counsels in favor of affirming the Fourth Circuit.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Gonzaga University v. Doe framework, which demands that a statutory provision unambiguously confer an individually enforceable right through rights-creating, individual-centric language with an unmistakable focus on the benefited class, 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23) is most naturally read as a condition imposed on States receiving Medicaid funds rather than an unambiguous conferral of a personal right on individual beneficiaries. As I noted in my Talevski concurrence, Spending Clause statutes operate as contracts between the federal government and the States, and the existence of a comprehensive enforcement mechanism in § 1396c — authorizing the Secretary to withhold funding from noncompliant States — is strong textual and structural evidence that Congress did not intend to supplement that scheme with private § 1983 enforcement. While Wilder and Blessing have not been formally overruled, Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Center and Talevski's reaffirmation of Gonzaga's 'demanding bar' substantially undermine their methodological premises, and the Fourth Circuit erred in mechanically reapplying those frameworks without rigorously interrogating whether the statutory text truly speaks in the voice of individual rights rather than programmatic conditions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1396a(a)(23) uses unmistakably individual-centric, rights-creating language — it provides that any individual 'eligible for medical assistance' may 'obtain such assistance from any institution, agency, community pharmacy, or person, qualified to perform the service,' which is precisely the kind of 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited' language Gonzaga and Talevski require for § 1983 enforceability. While the research confirms genuine circuit confusion about whether Gonzaga narrowed or merely restated the Blessing framework, Talevski's majority reaffirmed that Spending Clause statutes can create privately enforceable rights under § 1983 and did not overrule Wilder, which specifically upheld § 1983 enforcement of Medicaid provisions — and Justice Barrett's concurrence notably declined to declare Wilder invalid. From a practical consequences standpoint, relegating Medicaid beneficiaries solely to the Secretary's funding-withholding mechanism under § 1396c would leave vulnerable low-income patients without meaningful, timely recourse when states exclude qualified providers, effectively rendering the free-choice guarantee unenforceable at the individual level where it matters most. The existence of an administrative enforcement mechanism does not, under Talevski's framework, automatically foreclose § 1983 enforcement unless Congress made that mechanism sufficiently comprehensive and exclusive to demonstrate intent to preclude private suits — a showing South Carolina has not made here.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Medicaid beneficiaries have a privately enforceable right of action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 to challenge a State's exclusion of a Medicaid provider under the free-choice-of-provider provision, 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23) — the Medicaid 'free-choice-of-provider' provision — read in conjunction with 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which provides a cause of action for deprivation of federal statutory rights under color of state law.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: South Carolina (Petitioner) argues that § 1396a(a)(23) does not unambiguously confer an individually enforceable right upon Medicaid beneficiaries sufficient to sustain a § 1983 cause of action, and that the State retains authority to exclude providers it deems unqualified — such as Planned Parenthood South Atlantic — without triggering private litigation by beneficiaries. The Petitioner, supported by the United States as amicus and numerous state legislators, contends that enforcement of Medicaid compliance should rest exclusively with the federal government through administrative mechanisms, including withholding of federal funding under 42 U.S.C. § 1396c, rather than through private suits under § 1983.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Planned Parenthood South Atlantic (Respondent) argues that § 1396a(a)(23) unambiguously creates an individual right for Medicaid beneficiaries to obtain services from any qualified provider of their choosing, and that this right is privately enforceable through § 1983. Respondents contend that controlling precedents — including Wilder v. Virginia Hospital Ass'n and Blessing v. Freestone — establish the framework under which this provision confers enforceable rights, and that the Supreme Court's decision in Health and Hospital Corp. of Marion County v. Talevski (2023) reaffirmed rather than undermined the availability of § 1983 to enforce Medicaid statutory rights.
key_precedents: Wilder v. Virginia Hospital Ass'n, 496 U.S. 498 (1990) — established that Medicaid provisions can create privately enforceable rights under § 1983
Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997) — set out the three-part test for determining whether a federal statute confers an individually enforceable right under § 1983

Health and Hospital Corp. of Marion County v. Talevski, 599 U.S. 166 (2023) — reaffirmed that § 1983 remains available to enforce federal statutory rights, including specific FNHRA provisions under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1396a(a)(28) and 1396r

Gonzaga University v. Doe, 536 U.S. 273 (2002) — tightened the standard for finding individually enforceable rights, requiring that a statute unambiguously confer rights on a specific class of beneficiaries
Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. 137 (1803) — cited for the foundational principle that it is the judiciary's role to say what the law is
Kerr v. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic, 143 S. Ct. 2633 (2023) — the Supreme Court's GVR order vacating the Fourth Circuit's prior judgment and remanding for reconsideration in light of Talevski

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh have together sharpened the structural mismatch argument — that § 1396c's programmatic funding-withholding remedy cannot be 'comprehensive' in the Rancho Palos Verdes sense with respect to individual beneficiary claims — and I acknowledge this is a serious point that weakens the exclusive-remedy pillar of the petitioner position. However, my minimalist instinct leads me to a different narrow ground: the Pennhurst clear-statement principle requires not merely that the substantive right be individually focused, but that states have unmistakable notice at the time of accepting funds that they are exposed to private § 1983 litigation specifically, and the combination of § 1396a(a)(23)'s structural embedding as a plan-condition directive alongside § 1396c's remedial architecture creates genuine ambiguity about whether Congress intended to open the courthouse doors to individual suits rather than channeling enforcement through the Secretary. Justice Kagan is correct that Talevski rejected automatic preclusion, but Talevski does not resolve the distinct Pennhurst question of whether this particular statutory architecture provided states with sufficiently clear notice of private litigation exposure — and on that narrow ground, I would hold for petitioner while expressly reserving judgment on Medicaid provisions with more explicit individual-remedy language. I maintain my position with reduced confidence because the structural mismatch argument Justice Barrett identifies is genuinely compelling and I cannot dismiss it, but the Pennhurst clear-statement concern remains the load-bearing pillar of my analysis and has not been adequately answered.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson both emphasize that 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain' services constitutes rights-creating language satisfying Gonzaga, but this conflates rights-sounding language with the unambiguous conferral of individually enforceable rights that Gonzaga actually demands — the Court in Gonzaga explicitly warned against 'plucking out' isolated phrases and instructed examination of the entire statutory architecture. The comprehensive enforcement mechanism in § 1396c, which vests remedial authority exclusively in the Secretary through funding withholding, is precisely the kind of structural evidence Gonzaga instructs us to weigh, and it strongly suggests Congress channeled enforcement through federal administrative action rather than private litigation. Justice Sotomayor's policy argument that administrative enforcement is 'slow and uncertain' is not a textual or structural argument at all — it is an invitation to rewrite the statute based on preferred outcomes, which is antithetical to both textualism and the Pennhurst principle that spending conditions must be clear at the time of acceptance. Furthermore, the 'qualified provider' determination necessarily involves state administrative discretion, and allowing § 1983 suits to second-guess those determinations would fundamentally disrupt the cooperative federalism structure Congress designed, a concern Justice Kavanaugh rightly identifies even while acknowledging the case is close.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that § 1396c's programmatic remedy is structurally mismatched with individual entitlements remains the most sophisticated respondent argument, and I acknowledge Justice Kavanaugh's defection on this basis carries weight — but I cannot follow him there because the structural mismatch argument, however elegant, ultimately asks courts to supplement Congress's chosen enforcement architecture based on judicial assessments of remedy adequacy, which is precisely the kind of institutional overreach that Pennhurst's clear-statement principle guards against. Justice Kagan insists that Talevski forecloses my position, but Talevski held only that administrative schemes do not automatically preclude § 1983 — it did not hold that rights-adjacent language in a plan-condition directive automatically satisfies Gonzaga's demanding standard, and the question here is whether § 1396a(a)(23)'s primary function as a structural plan requirement, embedded in a comprehensive cooperative federalism scheme, reflects the unmistakable individual-rights conferral Gonzaga demands. Justice Jackson's textual argument about 'any individual... may obtain... of his choice' is forceful, but Gonzaga explicitly warned against plucking out isolated phrases, and the provision's structural context — as one of dozens of plan conditions enforceable through § 1396c — undermines the inference that Congress intended to create privately enforceable rights rather than federally administered program standards. I maintain my position because the Pennhurst principle requires that states have unambiguous notice of private litigation exposure, and the comprehensive administrative scheme in § 1396c, whatever its structural limitations as an individual remedy, reflects Congress's deliberate choice about enforcement architecture that courts should respect rather than supplement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that § 1396a(a)(23) is merely a spending condition rather than a rights-conferring provision is the strongest challenge to my position, but it founders on the statute's unmistakably individual-focused language — 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance... of his choice' — which is precisely the kind of beneficiary-centric, rights-creating text that Gonzaga distinguished from aggregate programmatic directives. Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize that § 1396c's administrative enforcement mechanism reflects Congress's chosen remedy, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, Talevski explicitly rejected the proposition that the mere existence of an administrative scheme automatically forecloses § 1983 — Congress must manifest clear intent to make that remedy exclusive, and nothing in § 1396c's text does so. The practical stakes reinforce my reading: Medicaid beneficiaries — disproportionately low-income women seeking reproductive healthcare — cannot wait months or years for federal funding-withholding proceedings to vindicate an immediate, individual healthcare need, and a statutory right without a timely remedy is no right at all. Justice Barrett's point that § 1396a(a)(23) is among the relatively rare Spending Clause provisions that clears Gonzaga's demanding bar is well-taken and consistent with the textual analysis that drives my conclusion.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most formidable challenge — that § 1396a(a)(23) is merely a spending condition and that § 1396c's comprehensive scheme reflects Congress's deliberate enforcement architecture — cannot overcome the textual reality that 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any institution... of his choice' is unmistakably beneficiary-centric language satisfying Gonzaga's demanding standard. Justice Barrett's structural insight, now reinforced by Justice Kavanaugh's conversion, crystallizes why § 1396c cannot be the exclusive remedy: a funding-withholding mechanism operating at the programmatic level is simply incapable of vindicating the personal, time-sensitive entitlement the statute confers — a state can lose federal funding while an individual beneficiary remains without her chosen provider. Justice Roberts' Pennhurst concern is serious but ultimately inverted: the clear-statement principle requires that states have notice of their obligations when accepting funds, and language guaranteeing that 'any individual... may obtain... of his choice' provides exactly that notice of an individual entitlement, not merely a programmatic directive. Talevski, which I joined, forecloses the automatic-preclusion argument, and nothing in § 1396c's text affirmatively manifests the congressional intent to make administrative enforcement exclusive that Rancho Palos Verdes requires.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas's structural argument — that § 1396c's comprehensive administrative scheme reflects Congress's deliberate enforcement architecture and that § 1396a(a)(23) is merely a spending condition rather than a rights-conferring provision — remains the most formidable challenge to my position, but it cannot overcome the textual reality that 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any institution... of his choice' is precisely the individual-focused, beneficiary-centric language Gonzaga distinguished from aggregate programmatic directives. Justice Barrett's point, which I find increasingly persuasive, that § 1396c operates at the programmatic funding level and is structurally incapable of vindicating the personal, time-sensitive entitlement § 1396a(a)(23) confers is decisive on the exclusive-remedy question — a remedy that addresses only aggregate funding compliance simply does not address the same injury as an individual beneficiary's exclusion from a provider of her choice, and Rancho Palos Verdes requires the remedial scheme to be sufficiently comprehensive with respect to the specific injury at issue. Justice Roberts' Pennhurst clear-statement concern is serious and reflects genuine institutional caution I share, but as Justice Kagan correctly observes, the clear-statement principle cuts toward respondents here because states accepting Medicaid funds received unmistakably individual-focused language putting them on notice of personal entitlements, not merely programmatic obligations. I joined Talevski for reasons I cannot abandon without a compelling textual or historical basis that the petitioner side has not supplied, and the collective deliberation has only reinforced my view that the textual and structural case for individual enforceability under § 1983 is stronger than the administrative-exclusivity argument.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas's structural argument — that § 1396c's comprehensive administrative scheme reflects Congress's deliberate enforcement architecture and that Gonzaga demands examination of the entire statutory structure rather than isolated phrases — remains the most formidable challenge to my current position, and I do not dismiss it lightly. However, Justice Barrett's point, which she grounded in her Talevski concurrence and which Justice Kagan reinforces, is ultimately dispositive for me: § 1396c's funding-withholding mechanism operates at the programmatic level and is structurally incapable of vindicating the personal, time-sensitive entitlement that 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain... of his choice' plainly confers — a state can lose federal funding while an individual beneficiary remains without a qualified provider of her choice, meaning the remedies address categorically different injuries. Justice Roberts' narrower Pennhurst clear-statement concern is the argument that most tempts me back toward petitioner, but as Justice Jackson observes, the phrase 'any individual... may obtain... of his choice' is about as unmistakable individual-entitlement language as Congress writes, and I cannot in good conscience hold that states lacked notice of private enforcement exposure when the text so plainly focuses on individual beneficiary rights. I maintain my respondent position at modest confidence, recognizing this is a genuinely close case where reasonable jurists applying the same methodology could reach different conclusions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most formidable challenge — that § 1396a(a)(23) functions as a spending condition rather than a rights-conferring provision, and that § 1396c's comprehensive scheme reflects Congress's deliberate enforcement architecture — remains the strongest opposing argument, but it cannot overcome the textual reality that 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any institution... of his choice' is precisely the beneficiary-centric, individually focused language that Gonzaga distinguished from aggregate programmatic directives. Justice Kavanaugh's conversion to the respondent position on structural grounds reinforces what I identified in my Talevski concurrence: a remedy operating exclusively at the programmatic funding level is not 'sufficiently comprehensive' under Rancho Palos Verdes to displace § 1983 with respect to individual beneficiary claims, because it addresses a categorically different injury — aggregate noncompliance — rather than the personal, time-sensitive entitlement the statute confers. Justice Roberts' residual concern about Pennhurst clear-statement notice deserves acknowledgment, but as I have maintained, the Pennhurst principle cuts toward respondents here: states accepting Medicaid funds who read 'any individual... may obtain... of his choice' had as clear a notice of individual entitlement as Spending Clause drafting permits, and the clear-statement rule cannot be weaponized to demand that Congress explicitly enumerate every enforcement mechanism in order to preserve rights it has unmistakably conferred. My confidence increases modestly to 0.75 because Justice Kavanaugh's structural analysis — grounded in the same Rancho Palos Verdes framework I have been applying — confirms that the exclusive-remedy argument, which was the petitioners' strongest position, fails at the structural level.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that § 1396a(a)(23) is merely a spending condition rather than a rights-conferring provision is the strongest challenge to my position, but it founders on the statute's actual text: the provision does not merely direct states to administer a program in a certain way — it guarantees that 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any institution... of his choice,' language that is unmistakably focused on the individual beneficiary's personal entitlement rather than aggregate programmatic compliance. Justice Kavanaugh's institutionalist concern about federalism and the § 1396c administrative remedy is serious, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, Talevski explicitly rejected the proposition that the mere existence of an administrative enforcement mechanism forecloses § 1983 — Congress must manifest clear intent to make that remedy exclusive, and nothing in § 1396c's text does so. Chief Justice Roberts's narrower framing — that Gonzaga demands unmistakable congressional intent to expose states to private litigation — actually cuts in favor of respondents here, because the phrase 'any individual... may obtain... of his choice' is about as unmistakable as statutory language gets in conferring an individual right. From my perspective as a jurist attentive to practical consequences for vulnerable populations, relegating Medicaid beneficiaries to the slow, programmatic, and politically contingent funding-withholding mechanism would render their statutory right effectively illusory in precisely the circumstances — arbitrary provider exclusions — where timely individual recourse matters most.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying the demanding Gonzaga University standard, § 1396a(a)(23) must unambiguously confer an individually enforceable right on a specific class of beneficiaries — not merely impose aggregate policy conditions on States accepting Medicaid funding. While the provision does use rights-conferring language regarding beneficiary choice, the federalism concerns articulated in Gonzaga and reinforced by Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Center counsel restraint: Congress must make unmistakably clear its intent to alter the constitutional balance between States and the Federal Government by exposing States to private litigation. The narrowest and most institutionally sound resolution is to hold that the comprehensive administrative enforcement mechanism under § 1396c — federal funding withholding — reflects Congress's chosen remedy, and that absent clearer textual evidence of congressional intent to create a privately enforceable individual right distinct from that scheme, § 1983 does not supply a cause of action here. This narrow holding preserves Talevski's reaffirmation of § 1983's availability where rights are unambiguously conferred, while respecting federalism and avoiding unnecessary expansion of private enforcement against States.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying the rigorous Gonzaga University standard, 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23) is most naturally read as a condition imposed upon States as a prerequisite for receiving federal Medicaid funding, not as an unambiguous conferral of individually enforceable rights upon a specific class of beneficiaries. The statute's structure — including Congress's deliberate choice to vest enforcement authority in the Secretary through funding withholding under § 1396c — strongly suggests that Congress did not intend to create a private right of action enforceable through § 1983, as Gonzaga instructs courts to examine the entire statutory architecture rather than isolated rights-sounding language. From an originalist and textualist perspective, § 1983's text reaches deprivations of rights 'secured by' federal law, and a spending condition that regulates state conduct as a funding prerequisite does not 'secure' an individual right in the constitutional sense contemplated by the Reconstruction-era Congress that enacted § 1983. Furthermore, Wilder and Blessing's multi-part balancing tests are in irreconcilable tension with both Gonzaga's demand for unambiguous rights-conferral and the foundational Pennhurst principle that spending conditions must be clear at the time of acceptance, and those precedents should be overruled or sharply limited.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Gonzaga University v. Doe, 536 U.S. 273 (2002), a federal statute must unambiguously confer rights on a specific class of beneficiaries with rights-creating language focused on the individual — not merely impose obligations on states as part of a broader regulatory scheme — before § 1983 enforcement is available. Section 1396a(a)(23) is structured as a condition on state Medicaid plans, directing that a state plan 'must' provide beneficiaries the opportunity to obtain services from any qualified provider; this is fundamentally a directive to states about program administration, not an unambiguous individual-rights-conferring provision of the kind Gonzaga demands. Furthermore, Congress established a comprehensive federal enforcement mechanism through 42 U.S.C. § 1396c, authorizing the Secretary to withhold federal funds from noncompliant states, which strongly suggests Congress intended administrative rather than private judicial enforcement — consistent with the principle in City of Rancho Palos Verdes v. Abrams that a comprehensive remedial scheme forecloses § 1983 supplementation. Allowing private § 1983 suits here would displace the federal-state cooperative framework Congress designed, expose states to litigation over provider qualification decisions that are inherently administrative and discretionary, and effectively nullify state authority to make reasonable determinations about provider fitness.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1396a(a)(23)'s language — guaranteeing Medicaid beneficiaries the right to obtain services from 'any qualified provider of their choice' — is precisely the kind of individually-focused, rights-creating language that Gonzaga University v. Doe requires, with its unmistakable focus on the benefited class of Medicaid recipients rather than a mere aggregate programmatic directive to states. Talevski reaffirmed that § 1983 remains a viable vehicle for enforcing Medicaid statutory rights and clarified that the Gonzaga standard, while demanding, is satisfied when a provision is 'phrased in terms of the persons benefited' with 'individual-centric language' — and the phrase 'of their choice' could hardly be more individually focused. Relegating enforcement exclusively to the federal government's funding-withholding mechanism under § 1396c would leave vulnerable Medicaid patients — often low-income women who depend on Planned Parenthood for essential reproductive healthcare — without any meaningful, timely remedy when states arbitrarily exclude qualified providers, effectively nullifying the right Congress plainly conferred. The practical reality that administrative enforcement is slow, uncertain, and structurally ill-suited to vindicate individual patients' immediate healthcare needs reinforces that Congress intended § 1983 to serve as the enforcement backstop for this individually-worded guarantee.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23) is unusually direct in conferring an individual right: it mandates that a State plan 'provide that any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any institution, agency, community pharmacy, or person, qualified to perform the service.' The use of 'any individual' combined with 'may obtain' is precisely the kind of rights-conferring, individually-focused language that Gonzaga distinguished from aggregate programmatic mandates — it speaks to a specific class of beneficiaries (Medicaid-eligible individuals) in terms of their personal entitlement, not merely as incidental beneficiaries of a funding condition. Talevski (2023) reaffirmed that § 1983 remains a viable vehicle for enforcing Medicaid statutory rights and declined to categorically foreclose such claims, and the structural parallel to the FNHRA provisions upheld in Talevski supports enforceability here. While South Carolina's argument that the federal funding-withholding mechanism under § 1396c provides an exclusive remedy has surface appeal, Talevski explicitly rejected the notion that the existence of an administrative enforcement scheme automatically forecloses § 1983, and nothing in § 1396a(a)(23)'s text or structure manifests the kind of comprehensive remedial scheme that would displace private enforcement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of § 1396a(a)(23) is unusually specific and rights-conferring: it states that 'any individual who is eligible for medical assistance' *may obtain* services 'from any institution, agency, community pharmacy, or person, qualified to perform the service.' This language focuses precisely on individual entitlements — using 'any individual' as the beneficiary class and 'may obtain' as the individual right — rather than merely articulating aggregate programmatic goals, which is exactly what Gonzaga University requires: that the statute 'unambiguously confer rights on a specific class of beneficiaries.' Unlike the reimbursement-rate provision in Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Center, which was framed as a directive to the State rather than a right-conferring guarantee to individuals, § 1396a(a)(23) speaks directly to what eligible individuals 'may' do. While I take seriously the federalism concerns embedded in Gonzaga's demanding bar and the argument that § 1396c's administrative enforcement mechanism suggests Congress intended to channel enforcement through federal agencies, the textual specificity here — individual beneficiaries, individual choice, qualified providers — satisfies even Gonzaga's heightened standard, and Talevski reaffirmed that § 1983 remains a viable vehicle for enforcing such unambiguously conferred Medicaid rights.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying the demanding Gonzaga standard, § 1396a(a)(23) must unambiguously confer an individually enforceable right on Medicaid beneficiaries — not merely impose a programmatic obligation on states — to sustain a § 1983 cause of action. While the provision does use rights-conferring language ('any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any institution, agency, community pharmacy, or person, qualified to perform the service'), the critical question post-Gonzaga is whether Congress manifested unmistakable intent to create a privately enforceable individual right rather than a condition of federal funding enforced through administrative mechanisms under § 1396c. The federalism concerns emphasized in Gonzaga and reaffirmed in Talevski counsel restraint here: states accepted Medicaid funding with notice that federal enforcement, not private litigation, would be the primary compliance mechanism, and the comprehensive administrative remedy structure in § 1396c suggests Congress did not intend to supplement it with § 1983 suits. As an institutionalist, I recognize this is a close case and that Talevski preserved rather than eliminated § 1983 enforcement of Medicaid rights, but the workability concerns and federalism principles ultimately tip the balance toward finding that enforcement authority rests with the federal government rather than individual beneficiaries.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Gonzaga standard as clarified by Talevski, § 1396a(a)(23)'s text — 'any individual eligible for medical assistance may obtain such assistance from any institution, agency, community pharmacy, or person, qualified to perform the service or services required' — employs unmistakably individual-focused, rights-creating language directed at a specific class of beneficiaries, not a mere aggregate policy directive. Unlike the FERPA provision in Gonzaga, which spoke to institutional policies without identifying individual right-holders, § 1396a(a)(23) uses the word 'any individual' and 'of his choice,' language that unambiguously confers a personal entitlement on Medicaid beneficiaries. While I have emphasized in my Talevski concurrence that Gonzaga sets a stringent, demanding bar that will infrequently be met, the free-choice-of-provider provision is among the relatively rare Spending Clause provisions that clears that bar because its explicit rights-creating language and individual focus satisfy Gonzaga's requirements. The existence of the § 1396c administrative enforcement mechanism does not, under Talevski's reaffirmation of the § 1983 framework, automatically foreclose private enforcement absent a showing that Congress intended that remedy to be exclusive.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The text of 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(23) unambiguously confers an individually enforceable right by focusing squarely on 'any individual eligible for medical assistance' and guaranteeing that such individuals 'may obtain' services from any qualified provider — precisely the rights-creating, beneficiary-focused language that Gonzaga University v. Doe and Talevski require. Under the Blessing v. Freestone three-part framework, the provision (1) was intended to benefit Medicaid recipients, (2) imposes a binding obligation on states rather than merely expressing an aggregate policy goal, and (3) is not so vague or amorphous as to preclude judicial enforcement. The Fourth Circuit correctly recognized that Talevski reaffirmed § 1983's availability to enforce Medicaid statutory rights and, if anything, strengthened the case for enforceability here by identifying analogous rights-creating language. From my perspective as a jurist attentive to procedural fairness and the practical consequences for vulnerable populations, relegating Medicaid beneficiaries solely to the federal funding-withholding mechanism under § 1396c would render their statutory right effectively illusory, since that administrative remedy operates at the programmatic level and provides no meaningful individual recourse when a state wrongfully excludes a qualified provider.
